title: Intel Stock Drops After $15 Billion Share Sale. Is AI Spending Getting Too Expensive?
detail:
Intel Stock Drops After $15 Billion Share Sale. Is AI Spending Getting Too Expensive?

Intel's $15 billion stock sale dilutes shareholders but avoids more debt as its 2026 capital spending forecast climbs above $20 billion.

Oracle shares fell 9% and Google turned free cash flow negative for the first time as AI infrastructure costs alarm investors across the sector.

Intel must prove AI investments generate returns above capital cost, or shareholders will have financed the boom while owning less of the company.

Don't wait: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just revealed his top 10 AI stocks. See the full list FREE now.

The AI boom is creating an unusual problem for investors: The companies spending the most to build the infrastructure behind it are increasingly being asked to prove that the spending will produce returns. 

Shutterstock

Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) has pursued an $84.75 billion equity raise, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) has turned to both debt and equity to fund its data-center expansion, and the five largest U.S. AI data-center builders have added roughly $350 billion of debt over five years, according to Bloomberg data reported by the Los Angeles Times. 

Now Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) is adding another wrinkle. It isn't borrowing $15 billion. It's selling stock.

Intel Is Choosing Dilution Over More Debt

Intel announced this morning that it plans to raise $15 billion through a public offering of common stock, with underwriters also receiving an option to purchase another $2.25 billion. The company said the proceeds will support general corporate purposes, including capital expenditures and working capital, as it expands to meet demand tied to AI compute and semiconductor manufacturing. The Wall Street Journal reported that Intel has already raised its 2026 capital-expenditure forecast from $18 billion to more than $20 billion.

The market's response was immediate: Intel shares are down more than 3% in morning trading today.

Let's be clear about what shareholders are seeing. Debt creates interest expense. Stock issuance creates dilution. Intel is effectively telling investors it would rather increase its share count than pile even more debt onto the balance sheet.

Don't wait: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just revealed his top 10 AI stocks. See the full list FREE now.

That's not necessarily the wrong decision. Intel issued $6.5 billion of senior notes in April, including bonds carrying coupons ranging from 4.65% to 6.20%. But shareholders still pay a price.

The bill for the AI revolution has arrived, and Intel is asking shareholders to foot a $15 billion tab to avoid a mounting debt trap. © 24/7 Wall St.

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC), the chip giant betting billions on a manufacturing comeback, launched a massive $15 billion stock offering Monday, and investors immediately hit the brakes. Shares dropped roughly 4.5% during the regular session. Underwriters can buy another $2.25 billion over the next 30 days, potentially swelling the deal to $17.25 billion. That is serious dilution. But Intel also needs serious money. The company is burning through capital as it races to expand advanced manufacturing, packaging and foundry capacity, so management is striking while the stock is hot and turning a monster rally into fresh cash.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 6 Warning Signs with INTC.

Is INTC fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

And hot might be an understatement. Intel shares had nearly tripled in 2026 before the offering, giving management a golden window to raise billions without taking on another mountain of debt. The business is finally showing some muscle too. Intel's second-quarter results showed revenue surging 25% to $16.1 billion. But there is a catch: this comeback is expensive. Intel lifted expected 2026 capital spending above $20 billion from $18 billion as it pours cash into advanced fabs, packaging and the future 14A process. The bet is enormous. Intel needs those factories to win meaningful outside customers, not simply become increasingly expensive monuments to its turnaround ambitions.

Intel Stock Drops 4.5% as $15 Billion Share Sale Hits · us.finance.gurufocus

That is where the valuation picture gets uncomfortable. GuruFocus puts Intel at $97.26 on Aug. 10 versus a GF Value estimate of just $31.34, meaning the stock is trading roughly 210.34% above GF Value. After a near-tripling of the shares, management is effectively cashing in some of that enthusiasm to finance the next stage of the turnaround. Smart timing? Absolutely. Cheap for existing shareholders? Not exactly. The expanded deal could equal roughly 3.5% of Intel's market value, making dilution impossible to shrug off. Intel now has more ammunition, but the market has already priced in a lot of success. The next leg higher will need something much harder than another capital raise: major foundry wins, tighter spending and proof that Intel can turn its manufacturing billions into real returns.

title: Qualcomm's Android Growth Number Has Left The Front Of The Story
detail:
Qualcomm's Android Growth Number Has Left The Front Of The Story
Trefis Team
Mon, August 10, 2026 at 11:14 AM EDT 3 min read
QCOM
NVDA
AVGO
INTC
TXN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by manseok_Kim on Pixabay

A metric management once put at the top of its quarterly summary now surfaces only when someone asks for it.

Qualcomm (QCOM) used to put a growth rate on Android revenue in its quarterly summary. That number is no longer at the front of the story. What sits there instead is a fiscal 2029 revenue target and a data center push whose first custom silicon revenue arrives in the December quarter. The Android growth rate a holder could check every quarter has been swapped for a target dated three fiscal years out.

The Android Line That Used To Open The Summary

In November 2024 the Android growth rate Qualcomm reported was above 20% year over year. The company no longer leads with that measure. Its July 29, 2026 prepared remarks carry no Android growth figure at all, and the single Android number on that call is a 20% year-over-year decline in QCT Android revenue, with an earnings impact of more than $1.50 a share, given in answer to a question about the handset market.

The $40 Billion Target That Took Its Place

The front of the story now belongs to the data center. Qualcomm's non-handset revenue target for fiscal 2029 now stands at $40 billion, up from a previous target of $22 billion. More than $15 billion of that is meant to come from data center. The hardware is real: wafer production has begun on the two custom silicon wins, and a first high-bandwidth compute part has completed tape-out. What there is not is a scoreboard. Those two wins start generating revenue in the December quarter; the $40 billion arrives, if it arrives, in fiscal 2029.

Memory Pressure And A Thinner Slice Of The Next iPhone

The area that went quiet is also the area under strain. QCT handset revenues were $5.1 billion in fiscal Q3 2026, more than half of the $9.9 billion Qualcomm reported for the period, and the company puts the pressure down to industry-wide memory dynamics in the global smartphone market. Its share of the coming iPhone launch is now expected to be materially lower than the prior estimate of 20%. Company-wide, revenue over the past twelve months grew 1.9%, against a three-year average pace of 4.8%. Sustained revenue growth is one of the qualities the Trefis High Quality Portfolio insists on in its holdings.

The Handset Line Is What Settles This

This leans concerning rather than alarming. The pivot itself is landing where it can be seen: fiscal Q3 2026 brought record automotive revenue of $1.6 billion, up 61% year over year, and the BMW win extends that work across model programs well into the next decade. The concern is narrower. The part of Qualcomm that pays the bills today is the part that lost its headline number, and the part meant to pay them later is the part that cannot be scored yet. Qualcomm trades at $167.86, about a third below its 52-week high of $250.10, so whether a fall that size is an opportunity or a warning is the live question. The reported result against management's own forecast of approximately $5.2 billion in QCT handset revenue for fiscal Q4 2026 is what settles it.

title: Micron Technology Stock Surged On A Shortage The Company Had Already Described
detail:
Micron Technology Stock Surged On A Shortage The Company Had Already Described
Trefis Team
Mon, August 10, 2026 at 10:53 AM EDT 3 min read
MU
WDC
INTC
AMD
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image by Cristian Ibarra from Pixabay

The memory shortage behind the run was laid out in Micron's own supply disclosures long before the price caught up.

Micron Technology (MU) stock is up 708% over the past year, and the easy explanation is that it caught the AI trade. The narrower truth is that the shortage that repriced memory was set out by the company itself, in disclosures about its own wafer capacity, months before the price moved.

Three Wafer Starts For Every One Of Ordinary DRAM

The earliest of those disclosures came in December 2024, when management put the manufacturing arithmetic on the record: producing a given quantity of bits as HBM3E, the high-bandwidth memory that feeds AI accelerators, takes about three wafer starts where conventional DRAM needs one. Every bit sold as HBM therefore consumed the wafer capacity of roughly three bits of ordinary DRAM. Management said at the same time that HBM was already pressuring non-HBM supply.

The Company Said Its Own Supply Would Fall Behind

By March 2025 the same thread had hardened into a forecast. Micron said its own supply growth in calendar 2025 would run below industry demand growth in both DRAM and NAND. The company's HBM output for calendar 2025 was already sold out. Micron was also shrinking the smaller of its two businesses on purpose, taking NAND wafer capacity down over 10% structurally by the end of fiscal 2025. Those were statements about Micron's own supply, not forecasts of demand: a supplier telling the market it had chosen to make less of the ordinary product.

The Quarter Where Scarcity Became Pricing Power

The arithmetic reached the income statement in fiscal Q3 2026. Revenue reached $41.5 billion, up 346% year over year, as DRAM prices rose in the low 60s percentage range sequentially, and Micron has guided fiscal Q4 2026 to a record $50 billion, give or take $1 billion. Scarcity is now written into contracts as well: 16 strategic customer agreements are signed, with $22 billion of customer cash deposits and related financial commitments projected under them. Memory does not usually hold economics like this. On a trailing-twelve-month basis as of fiscal Q3 2025, just before the run, net margin was 18.4% against a three-year average of -1.3%, a good reading sitting on three years that averaged a loss. Durable margins and cash generation are among the things the Trefis High Quality Portfolio insists on in its holdings, and memory has historically been a hard place to find either.

Readable In Advance, Impossible To Size

Were the signs actionable, or only obvious now? The mechanism was readable: anyone who took those disclosures seriously knew memory was heading into a shortage Micron's own supply plan would deepen rather than relieve. The magnitude was not. A stock does not multiply on a wafer ratio, and nothing said in December 2024 or March 2025 sized a move of this order. The peer returns point the same way: over the same window the S&P 500 returned 23% and NVDA returned 25%, while WDC returned 490%. This was memory scarcity repricing, not the AI trade lifting every chip name alike. The repeatable part is the habit, not the trade: read a company's own supply and outlook language before the price agrees with it, which is what a screen of companies whose guidance is climbing is for.

detail:
Intel shares fall after surprise $15 billion stock offering
Fiona Craig
Mon, August 10, 2026 at 10:03 AM EDT 2 min read
INTC
Trade Intel on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Intel Corporation (NASDAQ:INTC) shares dropped 4.6% after the semiconductor giant unexpectedly unveiled plans for a $15 billion underwritten public offering of common stock, raising concerns about dilution for existing shareholders.

The substantial capital raise is designed to give Intel additional financial flexibility as it continues its turnaround and invests heavily in areas expected to drive future growth. The company intends to use the net proceeds for general corporate purposes, capital expenditure and working capital.

Although issuing such a large amount of new equity will dilute current investors, some analysts view the decision as a practical way for Intel to strengthen its finances while its share price provides a favourable opportunity to raise capital.

Wolfe analyst Chris Caso said, "While the transaction appears dilutive to EPS, we nonetheless feel that an equity raise is a sensible option now, given the stock price."

AI demand supports Intel's investment plans

Intel pointed to strong and sustained customer demand for artificial intelligence computing as an important factor behind its decision to increase its financial resources.

The chipmaker is targeting several high-growth areas as it attempts to strengthen its competitive position across the semiconductor industry. Its priorities include physical AI, purpose-built silicon, advanced packaging and external wafer opportunities.

These initiatives form part of Intel's broader effort to capture increasing spending on AI infrastructure while expanding beyond its traditional processor businesses.

The additional capital could give the company greater capacity to fund manufacturing and technology investments while pursuing opportunities arising from growing demand for specialised computing hardware.

Intel stresses capital discipline despite major fundraising

Despite the scale of the proposed offering, Intel said it remains committed to disciplined capital allocation.

Management intends to match investment spending closely with demonstrated customer demand and defined return requirements rather than pursuing capacity expansion without sufficient commercial justification.

Protecting Intel's investment-grade credit rating also remains a priority as the company balances substantial capital requirements with the need to maintain financial flexibility.

The equity raise therefore provides additional funding without increasing debt at a time when Intel is investing heavily in its manufacturing capabilities and strategic growth initiatives.

Oil prices were higher, with front-month global benchmark North Sea Brent crude up 1.9% at $85.13 per barrel and US West Texas Intermediate crude 2% higher at $79.72 per barrel.

The economic calendar is vacant.

In other world markets, Japan's Nikkei closed 2.1% higher, Hong Kong's Hang Seng ended 1.1% higher, and China's Shanghai Composite finished 0.7% higher. Meanwhile, the UK's FTSE 100 was down 0.3%, and Germany's DAX index was 0.3% higher in Europe's early afternoon session.

In equities, SpaceX (SPCX) shares rose 1.3% after Reuters reported that retail investors sold shares for the first time last Friday since the June IPO. Meta Platforms (META) stock was up 1.9% after Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg called for lower US regulatory barriers for open-weight artificial intelligence models to help American companies compete with Chinese rivals.

Newmont (NEM) shares were 2.5% higher, while Barrick Mining (B) stock fell 6.2%, after the two companies said they agreed to contribute excluded properties, including Barrick's Fourmile and Newmont's Fiberline and Mike developments, to the Nevada Gold Mines joint venture, in an agreement wherein Newmont will pay Barrick $1.95 billion for the contribution of the properties.

On the losing side, Intel (INTC) shares dropped 4.1% after the company said it is offering $15 billion of common stock in a public offering. Cloudflare (NET) stock was 1.8% lower after the company said it plans to offer roughly $2.18 billion worth of convertible senior notes due 2031 through a private offering to institutional buyers.
